Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

OECDscaleup (development version)

New analysis: high-growth scalers and scalers to mid-caps

Not part of the original Stata package. run_scaler_analysis() runs both parts from the indicators panel and writes the sa_*_<country>.csv tables.

  • compute_top_scalers(): the fastest growers among the 20 % scalers (employment scalers by employment, turnover scalers by turnover), ranked each year on three 3-year indices (relative growth, absolute growth, Birch-Schreyer), with fixed tie-break chains; cut-offs top 50 and top 1, 5, 10 and 25 %, every cut-off reported for every cell. Acquisition-driven growth is left out; joint_growth = TRUE also requires the other variable to grow (both versions are written). Cells in the characteristics format, plus each cell’s share of gross job and turnover creation.
  • compute_midcap_transitions(): crossings into mid-cap status under three definitions, all reported: EU small mid-cap (Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099; firms jumping past its ceilings are a separate outcome), leaving the EU SME category (up to 3,000 employees) and 250+ employees. A crossing must be confirmed in the next year; nothing is imputed, a status that the data cannot decide is missing. Scalers, pool non-scalers and each top-scaler sample are followed from the start of their growth window (t-3), with exit as a competing event: cumulative incidence by years since entry, entry counts, crossings by calendar year, and a discrete-time logit hazard with firm-clustered errors, also net of the growth window. Diagnostics for choosing between the definitions: financial coverage per year and the at-risk years without a status.

Input data documented in the package

  • The OECD variable dictionary (Phase 3 spreadsheet) is now part of the package: the dataset variable_dictionary (one row per variable of base_financials, plants_RAW and trade_RAW, with definition, format, coding, source, SBS code, priority and notes) and two articles built from it, vignette("input-data") and vignette("input-trade-data"). The priorities were fill colours only in the spreadsheet and are now a column; exit_acq and exit_close are first-order nice-to-have. The sector codes are NACE Rev. 2 or Rev. 2.1 (the spreadsheet said “NACE 2.2”). Each variable also says what the package needs (required, optional, not used) and does with it, and whether it is a money variable (rescaled with financials_unit = "EUR") and has its negative values set to missing. A test keeps these columns in line with the build.
  • The error for a missing required column points to the articles instead of variable_dictionary_v1.xlsx / variable_dictionary_v2.xlsx.
  • check_inputs() checks a country’s input files (or data frames) against the dictionary before a run: what would stop the build (missing or mistyped required columns, duplicate firm-years, section letters that do not match the declared NACE revision, a money unit that does not fit EUR thousand, missing reference data), what looks wrong or will be lost (codings, code forms, groups outside their division, regions without a TL3 type, years without an exchange rate, trade values that look like euros) and what the build will do (missing shares, negative values set to missing, sectors left out, records that do not link to base_financials). The report holds counts, shares and years only, so it can be shared. It reads only the columns it checks.

NACE revision and money unit are declared (breaking: nace_revision is required)

  • N1 NACE Rev. 2.1: the sector rules (the sectors left out, the technology and A38 groupings) are written for NACE Rev. 2, and the Stata code left out sections A, K, O, T and U by letter. NACE Rev. 2.1 (statistics from reference year 2025) shifts the letters from K on, so Rev. 2.1 codes would have dropped ICT, administrative and other services and kept finance and public administration, without a warning. On a synthetic test, Rev. 2.1 input lost 13 % of the sample and 14 % of the scalers; a panel switching revision in mid-panel showed five times as many exits in the year before the switch. config_scaleup() now requires nace_revision ("2" or "2.1"; nace_rev21_from for a panel that switches). The build stops, with counts per year, when the section letters do not belong to their divisions under the declared revision, and converts Rev. 2.1 codes to Rev. 2 (repair of motor vehicles back to 45.2; the sale of motor vehicles and building development stay where Rev. 2.1 puts them, as three digits cannot tell them apart). The excluded sectors are now found by division (01-03, 64-66, 84, 97-99, the same in both revisions), by letter only where the division is missing: a firm with a missing section letter in an excluded division is now left out. On the real national panels used for validation, letters and divisions agree everywhere and the sample is unchanged.
  • N2 Money unit: the variable dictionary asks for EUR thousand, and the Stata code divided by 1000 for a fixed list of countries only (PT, ES, RO, SI, HU), so a panel delivered in euros by another country stayed in euros (levels such as turnover, productivity and wages 1000 times too large; growth rates and rankings unaffected). config_scaleup() gains financials_unit ("EUR thousand" or "EUR", default: that country list), and the build stops when the median turnover per employee of firms with 10-49 employees does not fit EUR thousand.
  • N3 findep_rat4 (investment financed externally, (capex - cash flow) / capex): a firm that does not invest has tangible fixed assets falling by exactly its depreciation, so capex is zero and the ratio missing. Once the values are divided by 1000 (and in Stata’s float storage) the three terms no longer cancel exactly, leaving a residue of about 1e-17 to 1e-7 of their size, so the ratio became +-1e16 instead of missing. This moved the medians of findep_rat4 in the characteristics tables for every rescaled country (PT, ES, RO, SI, HU); on one real panel, a third of the cells. A capex within 1e-6 of the size of its inputs now counts as zero, and the ratio no longer depends on the unit.

Faster, with less memory

  • The output stages copy only the columns they use. In particular, compute_contribution() no longer carries all of accounts_indicators through its balanced (firm x year) panel. Group statistics broadcast to firms use collapse instead of stats::ave(), the approximate medians and dominance shares use partial sorts, the trade panel groups by integer ids instead of pasted keys, and run_scaleup_pipeline() drops the raw input once the panel is built. Every output is unchanged (checked byte for byte on all reproduction scenarios, synthetic and real). On the real national panels used for validation the pipelines run 2.2 to 3 times faster, and the peak R heap is 20 to 50 % lower; the largest panel (5.7 GB of indicators in memory) now takes 14 minutes instead of 42 and peaks at 19 GB instead of 32 GB.

Stata bugs fixed

Each fix changes results relative to the Stata code (and to git tag stata-parity-v1_3); the change was checked to be limited to what the fix should touch.

  • S1 Jump filter: in a spike such as 20-200-20 (or a dip), the spike year is now blanked; Stata blanked the year after it. The 20-employee floor is applied to the average over the year before, the spike and the year after. This changes employment/turnover early on, so all outputs move.
  • S2 ind_a38: NACE divisions 69-75 are now grouped as D69T71, D72 and D73T75 instead of the aggregate D68T82, which is not an A38 group (68 stays D68, 77-82 stay D77T82).
  • S3 Small-region aggregation (AT, CA, HU, IT, NL, ES, RO): a TL1 region with no small TL2 region is no longer merged (Stata treated its missing share as +infinity). A TL1 whose TL2 regions are all small but have no HGET10 firm is still merged.
  • S4 Predictor types: a scaler with a missing (or small-cell) quartile of MFP, physical assets or average wage stays “Missing info” (9) or “<50 year-sector N” (50). Stata let Transformational/Expansionist (5/6), which require that none of the three is in the top quartile, overwrite them.
  • S5 Contribution: of Stata’s analysis years (2014, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021), only those whose t-3 lies inside the panel are used. A panel starting after 2011 no longer gets a 2014 window without t-3 data, where every firm counted as an entrant. The years themselves are those the documentation specifies.
  • S6 Predictor regressions are estimated only on firms that can be scalers under the dependent variable (its high-growth pool: 10+ employees at t-3, growth known) and have fewer than 250 employees at t-3. Stata used every firm present at t-3, so micro and 250+ firms counted as non-scalers.
  • S7 TL3 regions with typology “..” (no typology) now have a missing typology_UR; Stata reported them as a sixth group “..”. They still count in all other breakdowns and totals.
  • S8 Raw data with both age_cat and birth_year (Stata stopped with an error): birth_year now drives age, entry and L3age; the supplied age_cat is kept as the age category. An all-missing birth_year column counts as absent.
  • S9 Size boundaries follow the documented definitions, consistently: employers with fewer than 250 employees at t-3 (0 < L3employment < 250; Stata 1-249) for the characteristics and persistence samples, and fewer than 10 for micro (0 < L3employment < 10) for both the micro scalers (Stata 1 to < 10) and their comparison pool (Stata 1-9). Firms with fractional FTE such as 0.5, 9.5 or 249.5 are no longer left out, and a micro scaler always has its comparison pool.
  • S11 The predictors documentation now says that the “Strategic (productivity)” type uses the MFP level at t-3 (as the code always did, like the capital and wage types); the Stata documentation said “productivity growth”.
  • S12 The never-applying floor for negative MFP is removed (MFP is an exponential, so never negative). Labour share stays labour costs over turnover, as documented. No result changes.
  • S13, S14 The two Stata crashes (an unlabelled age_cat; no regression year in the panel, which also lost desc_predictors) never occurred in R; tests now pin that.
  • S15 tech_grad: divisions that Stata left without a group are assigned: 58-60 and 63 to Advanced services, 77 to Other services tradable, 90-94 and 96 to Other services non-tradable. 01-03, 64-66 and 84 stay unclassified, as in Stata.
  • S16 Rescaling to thousands (PT, ES, RO, SI, HU) now includes cash_flow and gross_profit, so financial-dependency ratio 4 no longer mixes units.
  • S17 A firm with an empty region code gets a missing region-sector pair (reg_techgrad). Stata excluded only ".", so an empty region formed a pseudo-region _<sector group>. Such firms still count in all other breakdowns and totals.

Trade package

  • New: the firm-level trade extension (Stata trade package v1.0, MASTER_OECD_trade.do). run_trade_pipeline() reads trade_RAW_<CT>.dta next to base_financials_<CT>.dta and writes trade_accounts_indicators_<CT>.dta and n16_trade_characteristics_p1/p2_<CT>.csv. The steps are build_trade_panel() (transactions to a firm-year panel), build_trade_accounts_indicators() (n0_2: the panel build of the second package, an earlier version of it, with exporter/importer flags, first-time exporters, heavy/light exporting scalers, sector_exporter and digit_sect) and compute_trade_characteristics() (n1_6).
  • n0_2 is a modified copy of n0_1, so both run through one shared body; the trade differences (PT-only rescaling, no region aggregation, no reg_techgrad, no D68T82, …) are switched on by the trade panel.
  • At git tag trade-parity-v1_0 the trade code reproduces the Stata code including its bugs; two of them make Stata stop, and R stops with the same cause: trade data without import (or export) rows and non-numeric product codes. Merged into the fixes: the Stata bugs fixed above apply to the trade outputs too, wherever the trade package shares the code (S1, S7-S9, S15, S16), and the trade-specific bugs below are fixed.

Trade package bugs fixed

  • T1 Units: the trade build rescales the financials for the same countries as the base package (PT, ES, RO, SI, HU; the Stata trade package did PT only, so the trade outputs of ES, RO, SI and HU mixed EUR with EUR thousand), including the export-revenue variables. The unit of trade_value is a setting, config_scaleup(trade_value_unit =): "EUR" (divided by 1000) or "EUR thousand"; by default EUR for PT and HU, as the Stata code assumed. The 1-thousand product threshold (T7) then always applies to EUR thousand.
  • T2 A firm in the trade file that only imports has export value 0 (a non-exporter), and one that only exports has import value 0; Stata left the value missing, so import-only firms dropped out of the exporter/non-exporter comparison and the share of importers among exporters was computed over two-way traders only. Values that were missing in the raw data stay missing.
  • T3 First-time exporters (y4_exporter): a firm that already exports in its first observed year may have exported before the data start, so while that year lies in t-3..t it is now missing (unknown) instead of a first-time exporter, unless that year is the firm’s entry year. Stata counted every firm exporting in the first data year as new, which strongly overstated the share in the early years.
  • T4 Trade data without import rows (or without export rows) no longer stop the run (Stata stopped at rename trade_value1). That flow is then unknown for every firm: its variables are missing, non-traders included.
  • T5 Products are told apart by their 6-character code as a string. Stata converted it to a number without force: a code with letters (e.g. a confidential code) stopped the run, and codes differing only in leading zeros were counted as one product.
  • T6 EU partners are counted by the EU membership of each year: the United Kingdom (GB or UK) up to and including 2020, Croatia from 2013. Stata used the EU-27 of 2020 in every year.
  • HGX (heavy exporting scalers) keeps >= half the HGT growth threshold, as the code always did; the documentation’s “more than 50 %” is the same in practice and is now worded “at least half”.

Verified against Stata

Outputs were compared with the original Stata code (package version 1.3) run in Stata 19.5, on 9 synthetic scenarios built to hit every branch and on one full national firm-level dataset (confidential). All 9 output tables match in every scenario (rows, keys, labels and counts exact; other values within a relative 1e-4). The R code now reproduces the Stata code including its known bugs (git tag stata-parity-v1_3); fixing those is a separate step, see “Known issues inherited from the Stata code” below. Two Stata crashes are not reproduced: R completes where Stata stops (S13, S14). Translation errors found and corrected:

  • Stata arithmetic: x/0, ln(0) and 0/0 are missing in Stata, not Inf/NaN. This changed HG flags (turnover 0 at t-3), the p1/p99 trimming of growth rates and labour productivity, MFP, the acquisition flag and the financial-dependency ratios.
  • Stata storage: gen stores float. Reproduced (stata_float()) where it decides a threshold, e.g. 8/10 > 0.8 is true in Stata.
  • Stata’s x^y is exp(y * ln(x)): firms growing at exactly 10%/20% a year are not high-growth firms in Stata (stata_pow()).
  • The HG pool no longer requires the growth ratio to exist.
  • "." in sector_1d/region_2d is missing, and never forms a ._<sector> region-sector pair; the ".." TL3 typology is kept as its own category.
  • L3age is created (it was missing, so median_L3age was absent).
  • log_added_value_emp is renamed to labour_prod as in Stata; the Solow intermediates va sl k slk l sll are kept.
  • Region aggregation reproduces Stata’s share_small > 0.5 with a missing share counting as true (Stata bug, reproduced on purpose).
  • Approximate medians of growth rates were means: summarise() evaluated the means first and overwrote the columns (characteristics and desc_predictors).
  • Transitions/evolutions/desc_predictors write value labels (FOLLOW, LEAD, type) as Stata’s export delimited does; desc_predictors labels ALL as “Total”.
  • Evolutions: entry_year/exit_year are missing where entry/exit is.
  • Contribution: the p2 table for exiting is written once (Stata skips the aggregate block when the detail block is empty).
  • Regressions: replaced fixest with an emulation of regress, robust (stata_regress_robust()): Stata’s term names (0b.L3size_cat, 3.L3region_2d, o.x, _cons), base and omitted rows, left-to-right collinearity handling, HC1 errors, no regression with fewer than 2 observations, dominance shares rounded to 4 decimals. Previously any warning dropped the model.
  • accounts_indicators_<CT>.dta is written with Stata’s labelled numeric categories and encode codes (byte order; typology_UR extends the label that comes with tl3_typology.dta).
  • fixest is no longer a dependency.
  • Plant counts: when base_financials already holds number_plants / multiplant (Stata saves the plant merge back into it, so a second run sees them), the counts from the plants file replace them where a firm-year has plant records and the existing values are kept elsewhere, as Stata’s merge does. R produced .x/.y duplicates and lost multiplant. Found on real data after the tag; fixed on master.
  • Float storage in the rescaling: Stata’s replace v = v/1000 keeps a float variable float (and promotes byte/int to float), so the rescaled financials are rounded to single precision when the input file stores them as float. run_scaleup_pipeline() now reads the storage types from the .dta header and rounds the same way; build_accounts_indicators() takes them as storage_types. The difference is tiny in the levels but is amplified in capex (findep_rat4) and the MFP inputs. Found on real data after the tag; fixed on master.

Known issues inherited from the Stata code

Reproduced on purpose at stata-parity-v1_3, and all addressed on the FixStataBugs branch (see “Stata bugs fixed” above). Method items were decided one by one against the package documentation.

  • S1 (fixed, see above) Jump filter: in a 20-200-20 spike the year after the spike is blanked, not the spike.
  • S2 (fixed, see above) ind_a38: D68T82 is assigned after D69T71, D72, D73T75, so divisions 69-75 all end up in D68T82.
  • S3 (fixed, see above) Region aggregation: a missing small-region share counts as above 0.5, so large TL1 regions are aggregated too.
  • S4 (fixed, see above) Predictor types 9 (“missing info”) and 50 (“<50 N”) are overwritten by types 5/6.
  • S5 (fixed, see above) Contribution: years are hard-coded (2014, 2017, 2019-2021, as documented); the computed first/last years are unused.
  • S6 (fixed, see above) Regression samples include firms that are not eligible to scale (fewer than 10 employees at t-3, or 250+).
  • S7 (fixed, see above) Regions with TL3 typology “..” form their own category.
  • S8 (fixed, see above) A user-supplied age_cat together with birth_year fails in Stata (gen birth_year on an existing variable).
  • S9 (fixed, see above) Fractional FTE between 9 and 10 at t-3: such a firm can be a micro scaler but is never in the micro comparison pool.
  • S10 (closed) Output file names differ from the documentation. R writes the documented n13_* names.
  • S11 (closed, see above) The documentation calls the productivity type “productivity growth”; the code uses the MFP level.
  • S12 (closed, see above) Labour share is labour costs over turnover, not value added (documented choice, kept); the MFP < 0 floor can never apply.
  • S13 (not in R, tested) Stata crashes when age_cat is supplied without value labels.
  • S14 (not in R, tested) Stata crashes when no regression can run, losing desc_predictors too.
  • S15 (fixed, see above) tech_grad: divisions 58-60 (except 582), 63, 77, 90-94 and 96 get no group (nor do 01-03, 64-66 and 84).
  • S16 (fixed, see above) Rescaling to thousands (PT, ES, RO, SI, HU) leaves out cash_flow, so financial-dependency ratio 4 mixes thousands with units.
  • S17 (fixed, see above) An empty region code forms a region-sector pair _<sector group> (only "." is excluded).

OECDscaleup 0.1.0

Initial release: a behaviour-preserving translation of the OECD Scale Up project’s “Second Package” Stata pipeline (MASTER_OECD_p2.do and its 5 worker .do files, version 1.0, scaleup@oecd.org) into R.

What this release contains

  • config_scaleup() — replaces the Stata global macros set in MASTER_OECD_p2.do.
  • build_accounts_indicators() — translates n0_1_accounts_indicators_v2.do.
  • compute_characteristics() — translates n1_3_characteristics.do.
  • compute_persistence() — translates n1_3_persistence.do (transitions + evolutions).
  • compute_contribution() — translates n1_3_contribution.do.
  • compute_predictors() — translates n1_3_predictors.do.
  • run_scaleup_pipeline() — file-I/O orchestrator mirroring MASTER_OECD_p2.do’s role; every function above it is a pure, independently-testable data transformation.
  • Bundled reference data tl3_typology and exchange_rates, carried over as-is from the OECD-supplied .dta files.
  • A documented country_patches lookup table replacing the 3 hardcoded country-list branches in the original n0_1_accounts_indicators_v2.do.

Translation notes

  • Ported via a structure-preserving pseudocode of the original Stata source (a working document of the translation, not part of this repository), not directly from the .do files.
  • Several Stata/R semantic gaps were identified and deliberately corrected for, each with a dedicated regression test: Stata’s non-propagating missing-value comparisons (stata_num()), replace ... if semantics under an unresolved condition (stata_replace()), Stata’s round-half-away- from-zero convention (round_half_up()), and Stata’s percentile algorithm (percentile_stata(), confirmed equivalent to R’s quantile(type = 2)).
  • The original has no automated test suite; the one existing behavioural spec (the confidentiality worked example in the source PDF, §4) informed this package’s dominance-share tests. Everything else is covered by new unit and integration tests built from synthetic fixtures, since the real firm microdata this pipeline processes is confidential and never ships with the package (the fixtures follow the OECD variable dictionary, now variable_dictionary).
  • No .dlg dialog files exist in the source package, so no Shiny GUI was built (there was nothing to recreate).
  • Known residual approximations, not exact-match verified against a live Stata run at the time: statar::xtile()’s tie-breaking at quartile boundaries, and fixest’s robust-standard-error small-sample adjustment (both since verified or replaced, see the development version above).
